Learning Objectives
Describe the incidence of periprosthetic joint infection after total knee arthroplasty.
Determine differences among various types of periprosthetic joint infections.
Identify studies used to diagnose periprosthetic joint infections.
Outline an appropriate treatment plan for periprosthetic joint infection based on the type of
infection.

Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is the most common indication for revision total knee
arthroplasty (TKA).
The risk of PJI after primary TKA (1% to 2%) is slightly higher than that after total hip
arthroplasty (0.3% to 1.3%).1
The risk of infection is higher after revision procedures (approximately 2% to 6% higher in
knees).
Risk factors
Postoperative wound complications, such as hematoma formation, persistent drainage,
dehiscence, or surgical site infection2-4
Immunocompromised status, such as history of malignancy, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus,
inflammatory conditions, or being treated with immune-modulating agents
Prior surgery in the affected joint, such as arthroscopy or arthroplasty
History of infection in the joint or adjacent bone
History of corticosteroid injection in the 3 months preceding surgery5
Prophylaxis: optimization of the patient and addressing modifiable risk factors are critical to
prevent infection. Timely (within 30 minutes) and weight-based administration of effective
antibiotic agents (eg, cephalosporin) also is critical in the prevention of infection. Evidence
suggests that the administration of an antibiotic other than a cephalosporin is associated with
an increased risk of PJI.6

Epidemiology
PJI is the leading cause of revision TKA and one of the most common reasons for revision
total hip arthroplasty. All orthopaedic surgeons must be familiar with PJI to properly
diagnose and manage patients in whom this unfortunate complication occurs after
arthroplasty. Knowledge of key risk factors for PJI is crucial for patient selection and
counseling before arthroplasty.

Pain at the implant site is the most common symptom of PJI; it is associated with infection in
more than 90% of patients.
Definition

Presentation and Etiology
Although the prior Musculoskeletal Infection Society and International Consensus
Meeting definitions helped standardize the diagnosis of PJI, these recommendations
were generated largely via expert opinion. A multi-institutional effort resulted in the
creation of a new PJI diagnostic scoring system, which is associated with improved
diagnostic performance and formal external validation compared with the current
International Consensus Meeting and Musculoskeletal Infection Society definitions. This
updated schema also incorporates newer diagnostic biomarkers and molecular tests,
which were not considered in the prior definition.7
Types of Musculoskeletal Infections
Classification
(Table 1)
Acute postoperative infection: an acute infection that occurs within 6 weeks after arthroplasty.
Frequently caused by Staphylococcus aureus, β-hemolytic Streptococcus, and gram-negative
bacteria. Purulent drainage and pain are common symptoms (Figure 1).
Late chronic infection: a chronic indolent infection that occurs 6 weeks or more after
arthroplasty. Frequently, late chronic infections are caused by less-virulent organisms,
including coagulase-negative staphylococci and Cutibacterium acnes.
Acute hematogenous infection: acute onset of symptoms in a previously well-functioning joint
caused by bacterial or fungal seeding of the joint from a remote source spread
hematogenously to the affected area of arthroplasty.

Proper classification of PJIs as acute, chronic, or hematogenous is crucial because
management is guided by this classification. Acute postoperative infections and acute
hematogenous infections may be managed via irrigation, débridement, and component
retention. Late chronic infections are commonly managed via implant removal and
antibiotic spacer placement, followed by second-stage reimplantation of revision
components.

hematogenous infections may be managed via irrigation, débridement, and component
retention. Late chronic infections are commonly managed via implant removal and

Diagnostic Studies
Patient History and Physical Examination
(Table 2)
A detailed patient history and physical examination may result in the diagnosis of PJI with
reasonable certainty; laboratory tests are performed to confirm the diagnosis.
Frequently, signs and symptoms of PJI overlap those of hematoma formation, aseptic
loosening of the prosthesis, or instability, necessitating additional diagnostic tests.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A careful patient history and a thorough physical examination are the first steps in
evaluating a patient for PJI. Non–trauma-related pain is a common symptom in patients
with a PJI. Loss of range of motion or a feeling of instability in the joint may be present in
patients with a PJI and should be elicited via the patient history and physical

Imaging Studies
Radiographic signs of PJI are rare but include the following (Figure 2):
Periosteal reaction
Scattered foci of osteolysis
Generalized bone resorption in the absence of implant wear
Radionuclide studies
If infection is clinically suspected but cannot be confirmed via repeat aspiration, then bone
scanning may be indicated.

Radionuclide studies are associated with a high sensitivity (99%) but a low specificity (30% to
40%) for the detection PJI.
Technetium Tc-99m scintigraphy detects inflammation, and indium In-111–labeled leukocyte
scans detect leukocytes in periprosthetic tissue.
A triple scan can distinguish infection from conditions associated with high metabolic activity,
such as fracture or bone remodeling, improving the specificity of PJI diagnosis to 95%.
Has largely fallen out of favor in current practice
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is not a common diagnostic tool for the detection of PJI but can be used in ambiguous
cases.
Capsular edema, periosteal reaction, lamellated hyperintense synovitis, and intramuscular
edema are concerning for PJI.8,9
Positron emission tomography (PET)
PET recently has been shown to play a role in the diagnosis of PJI, associated with a
sensitivity of 98% and a specificity of 98%.
PET can be performed with the use of fluorinated deoxyglucose, which travels to areas of
high metabolic activity.

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies are a useful adjuvant in the diagnosis of PJI. Radiographic signs of PJI
include periosteal reaction, osteolysis, and bone resorption; however, they may not
always be present. Advanced imaging studies, including MRIs, bone scans, and PET
scans, may aid in the diagnosis of PJI in patients in whom no joint fluid is obtained or in
whom the diagnosis is otherwise unclear. MRI findings may include edema, fluid
collection, periosteal reaction, and lamellated hyperintense synovitis.10 Bone scans are a
useful adjuvant in patients with a possible PJI and a non-diagnostic aspiration.

Serologic Tests
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are nonspecific
markers of inflammation that, in combination, are very useful as an initial screening tool in the
diagnosis of infection.
Although a combined ESR (>30 mm/hr) and CRP level (>10 mg/L) has been thought to be
associated with a high sensitivity for the detection of infection, recent studies have shown
that ESR and CRP levels may be normal in patients with a PJI caused by indolent organisms.
Therefore, other serum tests have been explored recently.
CRP levels normalize within 21 days postoperatively, whereas ESR may require as many as 90
days postoperatively to normalize.
Continued high CRP levels and ESR should increase suspicion for possible infection.
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a cytokine produced by activated monocytes and macrophages as part of
the inflammatory response.
IL-6 may be a faster and more sensitive laboratory marker for the detection of PJI because it
lies upstream of other markers in the acute phase inflammatory cascade.
IL-6 serum levels return to normal (<1 pg/mL) within approximately 2 to 3 days of
uncomplicated arthroplasty.
IL-6 has not yet gained widespread adoption because of wide variation in levels with an
unknown threshold, lack of easy accessibility, and costs.
D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product released in blood after fibrin clot breakdown by
plasmin.
Although a nonspecific marker that aids in screening for venous thromboembolism, D-dimer
has shown promise as a biomarker for the diagnosis of PJI and determining optimal time for
reimplantation in patients who undergo two-stage exchange arthroplasty.
A threshold of 850 ng/mL is the optimal cutoff value for the diagnosis of PJI.

Serologic Tests
Testing serologic markers should be obtained for every patient with a painful
arthroplasty implant in whom concern for PJI exists. The typical markers obtained
include ESR, CRP level, and white blood cell count. These markers are used as criteria to
define PJI. Particularly, CRP level may be useful because it should downtrend

positive in patients with a thromboembolism or PJI.
Joint Aspiration
Joint fluid aspiration is performed if infection is suspected (Video 2).
Aspiration is associated with a sensitivity ranging from 57% to 93% and a specificity ranging
from 88% to 100%. The sensitivity of aspiration can be improved via repeat aspiration.
For the acute period (<6 weeks postoperatively), a threshold of 10,000 white blood cells/μL and
greater than 90% polymorphonuclear neutrophils was recommended to diagnose PJI. For the
chronic postoperative period (>6 weeks), a threshold of more than 3,000 white blood cells/μL
and greater than 80% polymorphonuclear neutrophils is recommended by Musculoskeletal
Infection Society criteria. However, recent studies have demonstrated that the threshold levels
for aspiration may be lower than those previously described9,11 (Table 3).
The leukocyte esterase colorimetric chemical strip, which has been used to diagnose urinary
tract infection, is a low-cost, semiquantitative, point-of-service test that is 81% sensitive and
100% specific for the diagnosis of PJI, with a positive predictive value of 100% and negative
predictive value of 93%.
Alpha defensin is a naturally occurring antimicrobial peptide released from activated
neutrophils as part of the innate immune response to pathogens.
It has been shown to rise in response to low-virulence organisms and is unaffected by prior
antibiotic agent administration.
A meta-analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic characteristics with a pooled sensitivity of
97% and a specificity of 96%.12
Similar to a synovial white blood cell count, adverse reaction to metallic debris may confound
the interpretation of alpha defensin results.


Joint Aspiration
Joint aspiration is the mainstay of PJI diagnosis in patients in whom PJI is suspected. In
patients with a painful total hip arthroplasty or TKA implant who have elevated
inflammatory markers or in whom PJI is suspected, aspiration of the joint is a crucial
diagnostic step, adding critical data to aid in the diagnosis. A cell count is extremely
helpful and predictive of PJI in the acute and chronic settings (Table 3). Total white blood
cell count and percentage of polymorphonuclear neutrophils are crucial in determining
the likelihood of infection. In patients with a metal-on-metal implant, a manual cell count
is necessary to avoid spurious results secondary to soft-tissue debris.
In addition to a cell count, tests for alternative markers, including alpha-defensin and
leukocyte esterase, have increased in frequency. Continued research is necessary to

Microbiology
A definitive diagnosis can be made if the same pathogen is recovered from serial joint
aspiration or from at least two of three specimens of periprosthetic tissue obtained
intraoperatively.
With the increase in the number of biofilm-producing and slow-growing, fastidious organisms
(eg, C acnes), techniques for improving the accuracy of diagnosis of PJI include keeping cultures
for a minimum of 14 days and using enriched media for the culture of aspirate and tissue
specimens.
Histopathology
Gram staining is associated with an unacceptable level of sensitivity (0% to 23%) for the
detection of PJI; therefore, it is considered unreliable for diagnosis (ie, negative Gram stain
reveals little information, whereas a positive Gram stain is almost definitive for infection).
Frozen sections
Frozen sections are another valuable tool for the diagnosis of PJI.
They are most useful in equivocal cases in which preoperative investigations are confounded
by false increases in ESR and CRP level or if the intraoperative appearance of the joint may
indicate infection.
Most studies on frozen sections report favorable results, with a sensitivity of approximately
85% and a specificity of approximately 90% to 95%.
Current definition of positive histologic analysis of periprosthetic tissue: acute inflammation:
greater than 5 neutrophils/high power field in five high power fields (at 400x magnification)
Molecular Techniques
Conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of joint fluid aspirate
This technique relies on the amplification of bacterial DNA.

The test is so sensitive that contamination with a few bacteria may yield a false-positive

Custom PCR
Selective amplification of regions of DNA or ribosomal RNA
Multiplex PCR, with pan-genomic amplification of DNA and mass spectrometry, has improved
the accuracy of PCR for the diagnosis of PJI.
Occasionally, multiplex PCR was used to identify pathogenic bacteria in patients with culture-
negative PJI. This has been replaced mostly by next-generation sequencing.
Microarray technology
Microarray technology attempts to target specific bacterial genes.
It produces a profile of the genes (microarray) present in the joint aspirate or periarticular
tissues and relies on identifying signature genes/proteins that indicate infection.
This technology is not commonly used in clinical practice because of its variability and lack of
reliability.
Gene amplification (PCR or microarray technology)
Next-generation sequencing
High-throughput DNA sequencing. Dissimilar from PCR, next-generation sequencing can be
used in open mode, which does not rely on a set of parameters or a panel of primer targets.
It searches all microbial databases, including bacteria, viruses, yeast, fungi and parasites.
Next-generation sequencing can detect antimicrobial resistance via identification of known
resistance genes.

Molecular Techniques
Advanced molecular techniques, including PCR, microarray, and next-generation
sequencing are becoming more widely available for clinicians. These techniques allow for
detection of the genetic material of infectious organisms and have enormous potential
to identify causative organisms and polymicrobial infection if present. This is an
extremely active and promising area in PJI research.

Overview
Management of PJI usually involves multiple procedures.
Management also usually involves a prolonged course of antimicrobial therapy.
Characteristics of PJIs
Biofilm formation
Biofilm formation is characteristic of PJI because of certain organisms (eg, staphylococci,
Pseudomonas); the biofilm is believed to form and establish within 4 weeks.
Bacteria produce an extracellular matrix, such as a glycocalyx, that facilitates adherence to
the implant surface and acts as a defense against antibiotic agents and the host’s immune
system (Figure 3).
The diagnosis and eradication of PJI are difficult after the formation of a biofilm.
The sessile bacteria within a biofilm are phenotypically and metabolically distinct from their
planktonic counterparts because of differential gene expression.
For established infections, the removal of the prosthesis is recommended.
Early postoperative and acute hematogenous infections are less likely to be associated with
the development of a biofilm or prosthetic loosening; the likelihood of eradicating infection
without prosthetic removal is higher in these patients than in patients with indolent
disease.
Microbial colonization
Microbial colonization can occur at the time of prosthetic implantation.
It also can result from the direct spread of a pathogen from a contiguous focus or from
hematogenous seeding.

Surgical management
Débridement with retention of a prosthesis
Two-stage exchange arthroplasty: resection arthroplasty with planned reimplantation of a
new prosthesis
One-stage exchange arthroplasty has been gaining popularity in the United States as a
potential treatment option for acute and chronic PJIs in select groups of patients
Definitive resection arthroplasty
Arthrodesis (knee only)
Amputation
Nonsurgical management
Management: suppressive antimicrobial therapy
Indications: Considered in frail, elderly, and medically infirm patients in whom surgical
treatment is not possible or in patients who refuse surgical treatment


General Treatment Principles
In most patients, surgical treatment is the main method for the management of PJI
(Video 3). Acute PJI, including acute PJI that occurs within the first 6 weeks after primary
arthroplasty and the acute onset of a hematogenously spread PJI, can be managed via
débridement with retention of components. Chronic PJI mostly is managed via
débridement and resection of components. In rare patients, antibiotic suppression
without surgical management may be used; however, this approach is not as successful
at eliminating symptoms and additional infectious breakthroughs.

Surgical Management
Two-stage exchange/replacement arthroplasty is the preferred treatment option for chronic
PJI
Procedure
Removal of prosthesis
Surgical débridement of the joint
Placement of antibiotic spacer (Video 4)
Administration of antimicrobial agents with subsequent delayed reimplantation of the
prosthesis

techniques for revision total hip arthroplasty. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Prerequisites
Adequate patient bone stock
Medical fitness of the patient for multiple surgical procedures
Reimplantation relies on confirmation of infection control (declining serologic parameters,
wound healing, and negative microbiologic tests of joint aspirate if performed).

Antimicrobial agents are administered for 4 to 6 weeks after resection arthroplasty and
antibiotic spacer placement (Video 5).
Before reimplantation, antimicrobial therapy should be stopped for at least 2 weeks before
joint fluid aspiration and repeat serologies.
The interval between the removal of a prosthesis and reimplantation varies greatly.
No specific protocol exists for this two-step process; however, for PJI of a TKA implant,
reimplantation within 2 weeks is successful in approximately 35% of patients, compared
with success rates ranging from 70% to 90% in patients who undergo delayed
reimplantation (>6 weeks) and more extensive antimicrobial therapy.
The timing of reimplantation after parenteral antibiotic therapy should be based on the
clinical appearance of the wound and improvement in serologic markers of infection, such
as CRP level and ESR.
At the time of reimplantation, tissue specimens should be sent for culture with or without
histopathologic evaluation.
Reimplantation is indicated after all preoperative and intraoperative indices are
acceptable.
If a frozen tissue section indicates continued acute inflammation, then wound
débridement should be repeated, and a new cement spacer should be placed.

Antibiotic-impregnated spacers (static or dynamic) often are used in the interim between
prosthetic removal and reimplantation (Figure 4).
Dynamic spacers allow for joint motion and provide greater patient satisfaction and ease of
revision.
Static spacers allow for the delivery of higher doses of antibiotic agents; in addition, the lack
of motion may provide a more favorable environment for wound healing in patients with a
compromised soft-tissue envelope.
Dynamic and static spacers can become displaced and/or dislocated.
No difference in infection eradication rates exists between static and dynamic spacers. Some
data suggest improved final range of motion in knees managed via a dynamic spacer.

One-stage exchange/replacement arthroplasty
Procedure
All prosthetic components, infected bone, and soft tissue are excised.
The new prosthesis is implanted during the same surgical procedure during which the old
prosthesis is removed. For knees, the implant used in the European literature includes a
hinged construct because the technique described involves extensive débridement,
including the collateral ligaments (Video 6).
Antibiotic agents routinely are administered for a variable period after revision.
Indications
The procedure is more commonly performed in Europe than in the United States.
Local delivery of antibiotic agents often is recommended and achieved with antibiotic-
impregnated cement (if used).
The pathogen must be identified preoperatively to facilitate the appropriate selection of an
antibiotic-laden bone cement.
Contraindications to one-stage exchange12
Draining sinus or other substantial soft-tissue compromise
Peripheral vascular disease
Immunosuppression
Sepsis
Culture-negative infection
Methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA), methicillin-resistant S epidermidis, other multidrug-
resistant organisms, or polymicrobial infection
Reinfection
Advantages
Single procedure
Lower cost
Earlier mobility
Patient convenience
Disadvantage: risk of recurrent infection from residual microorganisms

No bone graft used

Procedure
Definitive removal of all infected components and tissue
No plan for subsequent implantation

Surgical Management
Two-stage exchange, which involves the removal of implants, débridement, and
antibiotic spacer placement following by a course of antibiotic agents and subsequent
reimplantation, is the most common method for the management of chronic PJI. The
success rate for eradication of PJI via this approach is variable, with multiple factors,
including host status, soft-tissue compromise, surgical technique, and causative
organism, contributing to reinfection. A dynamic or articulating spacer allows for
movement of the joint while the patient is between stages and facilitates surgical
dissection at the time of reimplantation; however, a static spacer may be preferred in
some patients with soft-tissue compromise.
One-stage exchange, in which the implants are resected, the tissues are débrided, and
then revision style implants are reimplanted during the same surgical event, is becoming
more common, particularly in Europe. One-stage exchange is appealing because it is
more convenient for patients and is associated with lower costs and resources. In
patients in whom two-stage exchange fails, particularly patients with soft-tissue
compromise in whom multiple attempts have failed, resection arthroplasty, arthrodesis,
and amputation are salvage options that may be considered. These treatment options
are reserved for rare patients in whom other options have been exhausted.

Antimicrobial therapy may be curative if an infected prosthesis/joint is removed and
periprosthetic tissue is adequately débrided.
To prevent false-negative results, antibiotic agents should be withheld until aspiration or
intraoperative cultures are obtained, unless overwhelming sepsis is present.
Initial empiric therapy for most common pathogens is a first-generation cephalosporin.
Vancomycin is preferred if any of the following factors are present:
True sensitivity to penicillin class of antibiotic agents
History of methicillin-resistant S aureus infection
Exposure to methicillin-resistant S aureus (in institutionalized patients)
Infection by an unidentified organism
After identification of the pathogen and susceptibility test results, the antibiotic regimen
should be tailored to the findings.
As part of two-stage exchange, antimicrobial-impregnated cement beads/spacers should be
used to provide high local concentrations of antibiotic agents in the periarticular space.
Antimicrobial agents should be administered systemically for a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks
between the first and second stage of two-stage exchange arthroplasty.
Bacteriophage Therapy
Lytic bacteriophages can penetrate biofilm and self-replicate within the host.14
Potential option for refractory PJI for which effective antibiotic agents are unavailable
Possible advantages: lytic bacteriophages highly specific toward their directed bacteria, no
cytotoxic effects to human cells, possible penetration of biofilm
Although in vitro studies are promising, limited in vivo studies are available to date.

Antibiotic Prophylaxis
The appropriate type, dose, and duration of antibiotic agents are crucial to the
successful management of PJI. Ideally, antibiotic agents should be administered in
consultation with an infectious disease specialist. Surgeons should routinely monitor
patients for the adverse effects of antibiotic agents and evaluate serum levels. The
selection of antibiotic agents for culture-negative infections may be difficult, and broad-
spectrum antibiotic agents are the main treatment option for such infections. The

Antimicrobial-Impregnated Devices
Antimicrobial-impregnated devices consist of solid spacers, beads, or dynamic spacers.
Doses of antibiotic agents in spacers
For each bag of Simplex (Stryker) prosthetic cement (40 g), as much as 3.6 g of an
aminoglycoside (such as tobramycin) and 3 g of vancomycin may be used for synergistic
elution kinetics. A maximum of 8 g (total weight of antibiotic combination) may be added
before the working property (such as moldability) of the cement is affected.
Gentamicin also is available in powder form at some institutions and may be used instead of
tobramycin.
The dose of antibiotic agent added to the cement should be based on the patient’s renal
function and the type of cement used. Palacos (Zimmer) cement provides better elution of
antibiotic agents than any other commercially available polymethyl methacrylate cement.15
For fungal infections, 150 mg of amphotericin-B or amphotericin -R or 300 to 600 mg of
voriconazole should be used (in addition to vancomycin and tobramycin) per batch of
cement.
Advantages of spacers
Reduce dead space
Provide joint stability
Deliver high local doses of antimicrobial agents
Disadvantages of spacers
Potential for allergic reactions or local or systemic toxicity
Potential for emergence of antibiotic-resistant organisms
Heat-labile antimicrobial agents cannot be added to prosthetic cement. (Tobramycin,
vancomycin, gentamicin powder, and amphotericin-B are heat-stable antimicrobial agents.)
High doses of antimicrobial agents may adversely affect the mechanical properties of bone
cement. This is an issue in definitive fixation during reimplantation but not in the temporary

Antimicrobial-Impregnated Devices
Selecting the appropriate antibiotic agents and doses to use in cement is crucial to the
effective management of PJI. Patient comorbidities should be considered because many
commonly used antibiotic agents in cement (eg, gentamicin and vancomycin) are
nephrotoxic. The type of cement used also will affect the elution properties of the
antibiotic agents used.
Conclusion
The preferred treatment option for the management of chronic PJI in the United States is two-
stage exchange. Although one-stage exchange is performed more commonly in Europe, the
results of this approach are not well established in North American patients. Ongoing studies will
help clarify if one-stage exchange is as effective or more effective at eradicating PJI compared
with two-stage exchange. The choice between a static or dynamic spacer is surgeon- and patient-
dependent; however, static spacers are preferred patients with an involved extensor mechanism
or a compromised soft-tissue envelope.
Management of recurrent PJI after failed two-stage exchange is a challenge. Revision two-stage
exchange after failed two-stage exchange is associated with a 42% recurrence of PJI.16
Consideration of resection arthroplasty, arthrodesis, or amputation is reserved for complex cases
in patients in whom multiple attempts at eradication have failed and patients with a
compromised soft-tissue envelope. Novel strategies, including bacteriophage therapy, may hold
promise in the future management of such refractory cases.
